name: TinyCC (tcc)
workload: Compiling the Links web browser from source (76,936 LOC, 1,950,947 LOC including headers, 67.2MB total)
claimed_speedup: TinyCC 0.9.22 compiles in 2.27s (859,000 lines/s, 29.6MB/s) vs GCC 3.2 -O0 in 20.0s (98,000 lines/s, 3.4MB/s) -- 'TinyCC is about 9 times faster than GCC'
compiler_and_flags: GCC 3.2 -O0 vs TinyCC 0.9.22 (tcc has no comparable optimization flags)
stars_or_usage: 3038 stars (GitHub mirror); used as a fast dev-mode C backend by projects such as the V language and QEMU's TCG interpreter lineage
tradeoffs: Minimal optimization (generated code roughly at gcc -O0/-O1 quality); partial C11/GNU-extension coverage; best suited to development/debug builds rather than production-optimized binaries
caveats: Benchmark is the project author's own page, using GCC 3.2 on a Pentium 4 (~2003-2005 era hardware/compiler); compares against gcc -O0, which per the evidence-tier rules caps this at C rather than A/B even though methodology (code sizes, timings) is stated; repo_url is an unofficial GitHub mirror -- canonical upstream is repo.or.cz/tinycc.git; a modern GCC/Clang would likely narrow the 9x gap.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fast C compiler" --sort stars, cross-referenced with the official bellard.org/tcc benchmark page

name: zapcc
workload: Full build of ETL (Expression Template Library, a header-only C++ template library) at -j1/-j2/-j4, debug and release configurations, link time excluded
claimed_speedup: Debug full build (-j1): GCC 5.4.0 469s, Clang 3.9 710s, Zapcc++ 214s -- 'zapcc is 3.3 times faster to compile than Clang and around 2 times faster than GCC'. Release build (-j1): GCC 782s, Clang 960s, Zapcc 640s -- 'zapcc is still 1.2 times faster than gcc and 1.5 times faster than clang'
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4.0, Clang 3.9, Zapcc++ (beta); default optimization flags, -j1/-j2/-j4 parallelism, debug and release configurations
hardware: Desktop machine, 4 physical cores, 16GB RAM (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires a persistent background caching server (zapccs) that consumes extra RAM; gains shrink for plain C or lightly-templated code; Windows/macOS support only lightly tested; sanitizers unsupported
caveats: Independent blog benchmark (2016) predates modern GCC/Clang by many major versions, and exact CPU model is not stated ('desktop, 4 physical cores'), so tier is capped at B, not A. A separate independent source, Colfax Research's 'A Performance-Based Comparison of C/C++ Compilers' (colfaxresearch.com/compiler-comparison, dated 2017, Xeon Platinum 8168, GCC 7.2.0/Clang 5.0.0/zapcc 1.0.1, -O3 -march=skylake-avx512), also ranks zapcc fastest ('handily beating the nearest competitor by more than 1.6x') but I could not confirm the exact per-compiler attribution precisely enough to cite verbatim, so it is noted only as corroboration. Project has been abandoned since 2020 (last merged with LLVM trunk 2018-02-13); GitHub reports license as NOASSERTION, README states the Illinois/NCSA license (OSI-approved).
found_via: GitHub: zapcc README FAQ benchmark links, found while researching fast-C/C++-compiler queries; cross-checked via WebFetch of baptiste-wicht.com and colfaxresearch.com

name: MIR / c2m (C2MIR)
workload: Compiling a single C function (Eratosthenes sieve, no #include headers) via the c2m JIT front-end vs gcc -O2/-O0, with gcc run against an in-memory filesystem to remove disk I/O
claimed_speedup: c2m -eg compiles in 336us vs gcc -O2 in 27.1ms (~80x) and gcc -O0 in 26.1ms (~77x); c2m-generated code then runs at about 92% of gcc -O2 speed on the same benchmark
tradeoffs: c2m targets lightweight JIT use cases: a short optimization pipeline, partial C11 + GCC-extension coverage, and no full preprocessor handling of complex real-world header trees in the quoted benchmark; general-purpose builds would see a smaller gap than the single-function test implies
caveats: This is the project's own README benchmark table (first-party with stated methodology), which per the rules is Tier C, not B. The workload is a single tiny function with zero #include files, and gcc is forced through a memory filesystem to remove I/O -- a best case for a minimal front-end, not representative of typical multi-file/header-heavy C builds. The table also directly compares against gcc -O0, which independently caps the tier at C; an 80x ratio is plausible only for this narrow synthetic case.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/vnmakarov/mir/readme, located while searching for lightweight/fast C JIT compiler front-ends

name: rustc_codegen_cranelift (cg_clif)
workload: Debug-mode cargo builds using the Cranelift codegen backend in place of rustc's default LLVM backend
claimed_speedup: README states the Cranelift backend 'has the potential to improve compilation times in debug mode' with no numbers given in-repo; project issue #878 ('Improve results on the rustc-perf benchmark suite') discusses roughly 10-60% (commonly cited around 40%) debug-build improvements on the rustc-perf suite, but I could not extract a citable numeric table from pages I was able to open this session
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; distributed as an official rustup component (rustc-codegen-cranelift-preview) for nightly Rust
tradeoffs: No SIMD support beyond std::simd (std::arch only partial), unwinding-on-panic is experimental and unsupported on Windows/macOS, recommended for debug builds only, still marked experimental overall
caveats: Used this run's one allowed Tier-D slot (project is clearly notable: official rust-lang org repo, rustup-distributed). The README makes only a qualitative claim with no numbers. The project's own rustc-perf.rust-lang.org comparison dashboard is JS-rendered and did not yield extractable figures via WebFetch in this session, and issue #878's numbers are rough/eyeballed from a chart image rather than a citable table -- a follow-up agent with rustc-perf's JSON API access could likely upgrade this to Tier A/B.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift/readme, and gh api search/issues "perf in:title" within the repo
